The retained information is intended to train and validate models that automatically flag accounts belonging to children, thereby helping the company enforce its age‑restriction policies. In exchange, Meta has committed to enhanced privacy safeguards, including stricter data‑access controls, regular audits, and a prohibition on using the retained data for advertising or other commercial purposes. The settlement also includes a financial component, with Meta agreeing to pay the participating states an undisclosed sum to cover past alleged violations of state child‑privacy statutes.

The agreement highlights a privacy trade‑off: while the retained data supports tools designed to protect minors from inappropriate content, it also means that personal information from children will continue to be stored by the platform. Observers note that the settlement sets a precedent for how large tech firms may balance regulatory compliance with the development of AI‑driven safety features, and it underscores ongoing scrutiny of data practices affecting young users.
author: TechCrunch

title: Bluesky introduces algorithmic opt-out feature to limit post reach
content:
Bluesky, the decentralized social‑media platform, announced that it will introduce a “followers‑only” posting option, noting that “sometimes people just want to post to their followers.” The new setting, which will appear as a toggle in the compose window, allows users to restrict the visibility of a post to the accounts that follow them, rather than broadcasting it to the broader network.

According to a Bluesky spokesperson, the feature responds to user requests for greater control over audience reach and aligns with the platform’s emphasis on privacy and community‑focused interaction. The rollout is slated to begin next week, initially for verified accounts, with a phased expansion to all users thereafter. Industry observers see the move as part of a wider trend among social networks to offer more granular audience controls, potentially shaping how creators and everyday users engage on the platform.
author: TechCrunch

title: Rivian CFO Claire McDonough to step down on Oct. 30
content:
Claire McDonough announced her resignation, effective October 30, according to a company filing released on Thursday. The filing states that McDonough is leaving the organization to pursue a new professional opportunity, though no further details about the role or the prospective employer were disclosed.

The company did not indicate any immediate impact on its operations and said it will begin a search for a successor in the coming weeks. Shareholders and employees have been informed that the transition will be managed to ensure continuity of leadership and ongoing projects.
author: TechCrunch

title: Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands airports suffer cyber‑attack affecting 8.7 million customers
content:
Manchester Airports Group (MAG), the operator of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports, said the recent cyber‑attack on its systems has not compromised passenger safety. The group confirmed that the breach, which affected the three hubs, involved unauthorized access to data linked to car‑park, lounge and fast‑track bookings as well as in‑airport Wi‑Fi sign‑ups.

MAG disclosed that the hackers obtained personal details for approximately 8.7 million customers, including email addresses, telephone numbers, vehicle registration numbers and postcodes. The company is working with law enforcement and cybersecurity specialists to investigate the incident and has implemented additional security measures while assuring travellers that airport operations and safety protocols remain fully functional.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Meta agrees to $18 billion settlement with US states over child‑addiction and safety claims
content:
Meta Platforms Inc. reached a settlement this week with 52 U.S. state attorneys general, agreeing to pay $18 billion over the next ten years without admitting liability. The agreement addresses allegations that Meta designed its Facebook and Instagram services to be addictive to children and misrepresented the safety of its products. While Meta denies any wrongdoing, the settlement also includes provisions that could trigger additional payments if other major technology firms, not named in the case, are found to have engaged in similar conduct.

The payout represents a small fraction of Meta’s recent financial performance, which generated roughly $60 billion in profit last year. More consequential, however, may be the requirement for Meta to modify or unwind certain platform mechanics that have been refined over two decades to maximize user engagement. Analysts suggest that these operational changes could have longer‑term effects on the company’s business model, even as the financial settlement itself is absorbed as a modest cost relative to its earnings.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Meta settlement impacts UK while other platforms remain silent
content:
Several major social‑media platforms have been approached by regulators and advocacy groups regarding recent concerns over content moderation practices, but a number of firms have not yet issued statements. The initial inquiries, sent earlier this month, sought clarification on how the companies enforce policies related to misinformation, hate speech, and user privacy. While some platforms provided brief responses outlining their existing compliance measures, others remain silent, prompting further scrutiny from oversight bodies.

Campaigners continue to press for more stringent standards, arguing that the current framework does not adequately protect vulnerable users. The debate among these groups remains active, with calls for legislative action and independent audits gaining momentum. As the discussion unfolds, authorities are expected to follow up with the non‑responsive firms, while stakeholders await clearer guidance on the next steps for industry regulation.
author: BBC Technology

title: UN urges broad social media reforms and California AG reviews teen safety on TikTok, YouTube
content:
California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta has announced that his office is now examining how TikTok and YouTube could be required to add new safety features for minors under the state’s Digital Safety Act. The move follows a series of hearings and public comment periods that highlighted growing concerns about the mental‑health impact of social‑media content on teens. Bonta’s office is reviewing the platforms’ current age‑verification protocols, content‑filtering algorithms, and parental‑control options to determine whether they meet the Act’s standards for protecting children online.

The proposed measures would mandate that both TikTok and YouTube implement stricter age‑verification checks, limit the visibility of potentially harmful content to users under 18, and provide parents with tools to monitor and restrict their children’s viewing habits. The AG’s office is also coordinating with the California Department of Justice’s Office of the Digital Safety Coordinator, which will oversee compliance and conduct audits of the platforms’ safety practices. Industry representatives have indicated that they are open to collaboration, though they have expressed concerns about the technical and financial burdens of rapid implementation.

If the AG’s recommendations are adopted, California would become the first state to enforce a comprehensive, platform‑specific digital‑safety framework for minors. The initiative is expected to set a precedent for other states and could spur broader regulatory changes across the social‑media industry. The AG’s office plans to release a detailed report on its findings and proposed enforcement actions later this year.
author: BBC Technology

title: Tech firms warn AI-driven cyber attacks will intensify within months
content:
A recent advisory letter issued by the National Cybersecurity Center has warned that cyber‑attacks employing artificial intelligence (AI) are expected to become significantly more sophisticated within the coming months. The letter, distributed to government agencies, financial institutions, and critical infrastructure operators, cites advances in machine‑learning models that can generate highly convincing phishing emails, craft malware that adapts to security defenses, and automate the exploitation of software vulnerabilities.

The notice highlights several emerging tactics. Attackers can now use AI to analyze vast amounts of publicly available data, identify weak points in corporate networks, and create customized malware payloads that bypass traditional signature‑based detection. In addition, the letter points to the rapid development of deep‑fake audio and video tools that could be used to manipulate executives or deceive authentication systems. Experts emphasize that the speed at which these tools are improving means that defensive measures must be updated continuously, and that organizations should invest in AI‑driven threat detection and employee training programs.

In conclusion, the advisory stresses that the window for preparing defenses against AI‑powered cyber threats is narrowing. It urges recipients to conduct immediate risk assessments, update incident‑response plans, and collaborate with industry partners to share threat intelligence. The letter serves as a stark reminder that as AI technologies evolve, so too do the methods of those who seek to exploit them.
author: BBC Technology

title: Qatar PM meets Iranian deputy foreign minister in Tehran to discuss de‑escalation
content:
Doha has announced an intensified diplomatic push to ease escalating regional tensions as direct talks between the United States and Iran remain at an impasse. Qatar’s foreign ministry said the Gulf state will increase its mediation activities, aiming to create conditions for dialogue and to prevent further deterioration of security in the Middle East. The move comes amid heightened concerns over the potential for conflict and the impact on global energy markets.

Qatar’s efforts are centered on three priorities: de‑escalation of hostilities, fostering direct communication between the parties, and restoring unrestricted navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for oil shipments. Officials indicated that Doha will coordinate with regional actors and international partners to facilitate confidence‑building measures and to ensure the free flow of commerce. The Qatari government affirmed its commitment to diplomatic solutions as the primary means of stabilizing the area.
author: Euronews

title: Draghi's Rhine Group aims to propose solutions for Europe, executive director says
content:
Draghi’s newly formed Rhine Group has set out to tackle a range of European challenges, from economic instability to climate policy. In a recent Euronews interview, Executive Director Luis Garicano explained that the initiative, named after the Rhine River—a long‑standing symbol of European cooperation—seeks to bring together senior policymakers, business leaders, and academics to craft actionable reforms for the continent.

According to Garicano, the group’s core mission is to provide a platform for evidence‑based policy proposals that can be adopted by EU institutions and member states. Its membership includes former heads of state, ex‑CEOs of major European firms, and leading scholars in economics and public policy. The timing, he noted, is critical: the EU is grappling with post‑pandemic recovery, the fallout of the Russia‑Ukraine conflict, and mounting pressure to accelerate green and digital transitions. By convening a diverse coalition of experts, the Rhine Group aims to offer coordinated solutions that address both immediate crises and long‑term structural weaknesses.

While the group is still in its early stages, Garicano emphasized that its influence will depend on the willingness of EU leaders to adopt its recommendations. If the Rhine Group can successfully translate its research into concrete policy measures, it could play a pivotal role in shaping the next decade of European governance and economic resilience.
author: Euronews

title: Malaysia plans September repatriation of Myanmar nationals
content:
Malaysia currently hosts more than 215,000 refugees and asylum seekers who are registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). The country’s refugee population includes a significant number of individuals from conflict‑affected regions, with the largest group being the Rohingya from Myanmar. According to UNHCR data, over 126,000 Rohingya are registered in Malaysia, making them the country’s largest refugee community.

The figures reflect Malaysia’s role as a transit and destination country for displaced persons, despite the nation not being a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Registration with UNHCR allows refugees to access limited humanitarian assistance and legal protection, though many remain in a state of legal uncertainty. The high concentration of Rohingya in Malaysia underscores the ongoing displacement crisis originating from Myanmar’s persecution of the ethnic minority.

These numbers highlight the continued need for international cooperation and support to address the humanitarian situation of refugees in Malaysia. While the government provides basic services through UNHCR coordination, the large registered population indicates a sustained demand for long‑term solutions and resources to manage the refugee influx.
author: Euronews

title: Piracy incidents off Somalia rise in 2026, IMO data shows
content:
The Iranian conflict that erupted on 28 February has already begun to strain one of the world’s most critical maritime corridors. Shipping lanes that traverse the Persian Gulf, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, have experienced significant disruptions as vessels navigate heightened security risks and uncertain navigation conditions.

Since the war’s onset, the region’s heavy traffic—home to a substantial share of global oil and commodity shipments—has been impeded. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a quarter of the world’s petroleum passes, has seen increased delays, rerouting, and heightened insurance costs. Maritime authorities and shipping companies are monitoring the situation closely, as any further escalation could widen the ripple effects across international trade routes.

In summary, the conflict’s impact on maritime traffic underscores the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz. Continued instability in the area threatens to disrupt global supply chains, prompting stakeholders to seek alternative routes and contingency plans while diplomatic efforts aim to restore calm.
author: Euronews

title: Flash flood engulfs China's Gyirong port on Aug 26
content:
On 26 August, a flash flood struck China’s Gyirong port, a key border trade hub on the China‑Nepal frontier, following a major disaster that had recently unfolded in Nepal. The sudden surge of water and debris inundated the port’s facilities, disrupting operations and damaging infrastructure.

Video footage released by local authorities shows thick mud and fallen trees covering the docks and warehouses, while trucks and cargo containers were swept away or left stranded. The flood was triggered by heavy rainfall that followed the earthquake‑induced landslides in Nepal, which have caused widespread flooding across the region. Gyirong’s strategic position on the trade corridor between the two countries means the incident could delay shipments and affect supply chains that rely on this crossing.

Chinese officials have mobilized emergency crews to clear the debris and restore connectivity, while both governments are assessing the extent of the damage. The incident underscores the vulnerability of border infrastructure to sudden natural events and the need for coordinated disaster‑management efforts in the area.
author: Euronews

title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
content:
Donald Trump signed an executive order today that will rename the portion of Lake Ontario within U.S. borders to “Lake America.” The directive is part of a broader effort by the administration to assert American sovereignty over shared resources amid escalating trade tensions with Canada. The order, issued under the President’s authority to manage U.S. water resources, will take effect once the relevant federal agencies complete the necessary administrative procedures.

The move follows a series of disputes over tariffs, fishing rights, and the Canada‑US‑Mexico Agreement (USMCA) that have strained relations between the two countries. While the name change does not alter the legal status of the waterway, it signals a symbolic assertion of American interests in a region long governed by bilateral agreements. Canadian officials have not yet responded formally, but the decision is expected to prompt diplomatic discussions on cross‑border water management.

The renaming is unlikely to affect everyday navigation or commercial activity on the lake, but it underscores the administration’s willingness to use executive power to address perceived Canadian encroachments. As trade negotiations continue, the U.S. and Canada may need to address the symbolic gesture in future talks to avoid further escalation.
author: Euronews

title: Nearly 400 dead, 1,400 missing after Nepal-Tibet floods caused by glacial collapse
content:
The U.S. Geological Survey reported that a recent disaster was the result of a glacial collapse that unleashed a massive flow of icy debris. The event unfolded in a remote mountainous area of the western United States, where the sudden release of frozen material overwhelmed downstream valleys and triggered extensive flooding and landslides.

Emergency officials confirmed that the debris flow damaged infrastructure, disrupted transportation routes, and forced the evacuation of nearby communities. Search and rescue teams, along with federal and state agencies, are conducting assessments and providing aid to affected residents. The USGS continues to monitor the glacier for further instability while investigators compile data to better understand the mechanisms behind the collapse.
author: Euronews

title: Protests persist in Azad Kashmir despite repression and internet blackout
content:
Protests that have rattled Pakistan‑administered Kashmir since early June have persisted through the region’s local legislative elections in July and August. Authorities have intensified crackdowns, deploying security forces to suppress demonstrations and arresting opposition figures. The government has also cut internet access and limited foreign media coverage, forcing residents to rely on local channels and word‑of‑mouth to document the unfolding events.

Amid the electoral process, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for a return to normalcy and an end to the heavy-handed tactics. However, the electoral commission reported a low voter turnout, citing fears of intimidation and the lack of reliable communication infrastructure. Human rights observers warn that the combination of restricted media access and the suppression of dissent could undermine the legitimacy of the elections and further inflame tensions in the disputed territory.

The continued unrest and the curtailment of information flow underscore the fragile political climate in Kashmir. As the region moves beyond the election period, the international community remains watchful, urging a de‑escalation of violence and the restoration of free press to ensure that the voices of ordinary residents are heard.
author: France 24

title: UEFA to file criminal complaint against FIFA president over failed World Cup revenue sale
content:
The Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) has announced that it will file a criminal complaint in Swiss courts against FIFA president Gianni Infantino. The complaint concerns Infantino’s aborted attempt to sell a stake in World Cup revenue to a group of investors that included Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital. UEFA’s legal team has described the proposed sale price of $4.2 billion as a “fraudulently off‑market price,” arguing that the deal was not conducted at fair market value and violated FIFA’s internal regulations.

The complaint follows UEFA’s investigation into the negotiations, which revealed that the proposed stake sale would have granted investors preferential access to World Cup earnings, a move that UEFA claims undermined the integrity of the competition’s commercial framework. UEFA’s lawyers contend that the transaction would have breached FIFA’s statutes and fiduciary duties, and that Infantino’s role in orchestrating the deal constitutes a criminal offence under Swiss law. UEFA has requested that Swiss authorities prosecute Infantino for fraud and breach of fiduciary duty, and it has indicated that it will provide all relevant documentation to support the case.
author: France 24

title: PSG drawn to host Manchester City and travel to Barcelona in Champions League
content:
Paris Saint Germain, the two‑time defending champions, will open their Champions League campaign at home against Manchester City after the 36‑team draw was announced on Thursday. The French side will then travel to Barcelona for their second group‑stage match, setting up a high‑profile clash with one of Europe’s most decorated clubs.  

The draw also saw Real Madrid drawn against Inter Milan, while Arsenal will face a yet‑to‑be‑announced opponent. The new format, which expands the competition to 36 teams, creates a mix of familiar rivalries and fresh encounters, offering a broad range of tactical battles across Europe’s elite clubs.  

With the group stage fixtures now confirmed, PSG’s supporters can anticipate a challenging opening tie at Parc des Princes, followed by a trip to Camp Nou, while Real Madrid and Arsenal prepare for their respective opponents in the coming weeks. The draw has set the stage for a compelling first phase of the tournament.
author: France 24

title: Trump Pushes $100,000 Fee for H-1B Visa Employers
content:
US President Donald Trump has announced a proposal to impose a $100,000 fee on employers who wish to hire skilled temporary foreign workers under the H‑1B visa program. The move would add a significant cost to the process, potentially discouraging companies from using the visa to fill technical positions. The proposal comes amid ongoing debates over the role of the H‑1B program in the United States labor market.

Tech leaders, including Elon Musk, have defended the program as essential for attracting top global talent to Silicon Valley and maintaining the United States’ competitive edge in innovation. In contrast, critics on both the left and right argue that the H‑1B system is often exploited to replace qualified U.S. workers with cheaper, more controllable foreign labor. They contend that the scheme can undermine domestic employment opportunities and wage levels for American professionals.

If enacted, the fee would likely reshape how U.S. employers approach hiring through the H‑1B program, potentially reducing the number of foreign applicants and shifting the balance toward domestic labor. The proposal remains under review, and its impact on the tech industry and broader workforce will be closely watched in the coming months.
author: France 24

title: Red Cross launches emergency response in Nepal after floods destroy villages
content:
François Picard welcomed Tommaso Della Longa, spokesperson for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), as the humanitarian agency intensified its response to the recent disaster in Nepal. Della Longa highlighted that the immediate challenge extends beyond the sheer scale of destruction; the loss of roads, bridges and communications networks has made it exceedingly difficult to reach isolated communities that have been cut off by flood‑washed terrain.

The IFRC’s priority in the affected regions remains search and rescue operations and the rapid delivery of life‑saving assistance, while simultaneously laying the groundwork for longer‑term recovery efforts. Coordination with local Red Cross volunteers is central to this strategy, as these responders are on the front lines providing aid to their own neighborhoods despite many having lost homes or family members in the crisis.

The situation underscores a dual humanitarian burden: the urgent need to address physical devastation and the personal toll on first responders who are simultaneously victims and caregivers. The IFRC and its partners continue to mobilize resources to restore essential services and support the resilience of Nepal’s communities in the weeks ahead.
author: France 24

title: Seven French presidential candidates hold first debate ahead of 2027 election
content:
Seven of France’s leading presidential hopefuls faced each other in a televised debate on Thursday, marking the first collective appearance of the field ahead of the 2027 election. The candidates, representing a spectrum from the left to the right, exchanged pointed questions on economic policy, security, and Europe, underscoring the increasingly tight and crowded contest that will determine France’s next leader. The debate, organized by a major broadcaster, lasted ninety minutes and was followed by a live audience of political analysts who noted the intensity of the exchanges.

The event comes less than eight months before voters head to the polls to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, who is completing the maximum two consecutive terms permitted under French law. As the campaign period intensifies, the debate is expected to shape voter perceptions and influence the strategies of the remaining candidates as they seek to consolidate support ahead of the final round of campaigning.
author: France 24

title: Nigeria kidnapping report released; Tanzania ousts vice‑president; Senegal launches local sickle‑cell drug
content:
A Lagos-based analyst has released a new report detailing the scale of abductions in the city, citing data that shows a sharp rise in incidents over the past year. The study, presented during a televised interview, outlines the demographics of victims, the most common locations for abductions, and the economic impact on families and local businesses. Analysts say the report could inform police strategy and community outreach programs aimed at reducing the crime.

In Tanzania, the ruling party has removed its vice‑president from office following his announcement that he would resign next week. Party officials cited a breach of internal protocols as the reason for the dismissal, although no formal charges have been filed. The move comes amid growing scrutiny of the party’s leadership structure and has sparked debate over the stability of the current administration.

Meanwhile, Senegal has announced the launch of the first African‑manufactured generic drug for sickle cell disease. The medication, produced locally, is expected to lower treatment costs and reduce dependence on imported therapies. Health officials anticipate that the new drug will improve access to care for patients across the country and could serve as a model for other African nations seeking to strengthen their pharmaceutical industries.
author: France 24

title: DW Survey Reveals Growing Discontent Among Russians Amid Economic Pressure
content:
Official polling indicates that public sentiment in Russia is on a downward trend, with a growing number of respondents expressing dissatisfaction amid mounting economic pressures. The latest survey, conducted by a leading Russian polling institute, shows a significant drop in approval ratings for the government and a rise in concerns over inflation, unemployment, and the cost of living. Analysts suggest that the tightening of monetary policy and the decline in commodity prices have amplified everyday financial strain for many Russians.

In response to these findings, Deutsche Welle (DW) reached out to its audience, inviting users to share personal experiences of how the economic situation has affected their lives. The broadcaster collected a range of anecdotes, from difficulties in affording basic goods to increased reliance on informal savings networks. DW’s initiative aims to provide a grassroots perspective on the broader economic trends highlighted by the poll, offering context for policymakers and international observers.

The convergence of official polling data and citizen testimony underscores a widening gap between economic realities and public confidence. As Russia navigates a challenging fiscal landscape, the growing discontent may prompt authorities to reassess policies aimed at stabilizing the economy and restoring public trust.
author: DW World

title: AfD poised to lead Saxony-Anhalt election, prompting migrant concerns
content:
The upcoming state election in Saxony‑Anhalt on September 6 could mark a historic moment for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), which is poised to become the first far‑right party to lead a German state government if it secures a governing coalition. Polls ahead of the vote show the AfD close to overtaking the incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD), while the Greens and liberal FDP remain marginal. The prospect of an AfD‑led administration has drawn national attention because it would be the first time the party moves from opposition to executive power at the state level.

For residents with migration backgrounds, the election raises questions about belonging, security and long‑term prospects in Germany. Many in the state’s sizable Turkish, Polish and Syrian communities have expressed concern that an AfD government could prioritize stricter immigration controls and adopt a tougher stance on law‑and‑order policies, potentially affecting integration programs and public safety initiatives. Local NGOs and municipal authorities have warned that heightened political polarization could undermine trust between migrant populations and state institutions, influencing everything from housing assistance to employment services.

The outcome of the September 6 vote will therefore shape not only the political landscape of Saxony‑Anhalt but also the broader discourse on integration and social cohesion in Germany. A victory for the AfD would test the capacity of state institutions to address the concerns of migrant residents while maintaining public order, whereas a continuation of the current coalition would preserve the existing policy trajectory. Observers will watch the results closely for indications of how Germany’s regional politics may evolve in response to shifting voter sentiments.
author: DW World

title: US sanctions on Iran weighed against China relations
content:
Washington is intensifying economic pressure on Iran while simultaneously working to ease political tensions with China. The United States has expanded sanctions targeting Tehran’s oil exports, banking sector and procurement networks, aiming to curtail the country’s revenue streams and limit its ability to fund regional activities. These moves follow a broader strategy to reinforce the limits imposed by the 2015 nuclear agreement and to compel Iran to return to full compliance with international non‑proliferation obligations.

At the same time, American officials are engaging Chinese counterparts to mitigate friction over trade, technology and security issues, recognizing that Beijing’s influence in Tehran could complicate enforcement of U.S. measures. Diplomatic channels have been used to encourage China to deny Iranian entities access to its financial system and to coordinate on secondary sanctions. By balancing heightened pressure on Iran with a measured approach toward China, Washington aims to sustain its sanctions regime without provoking a broader geopolitical confrontation.
author: DW World

title: Former Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic Dies at 84
content:
A former Bosnian Serb general has been found guilty of genocide by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), marking a landmark ruling in the aftermath of the 1992‑95 Bosnian war. The verdict, delivered on Thursday, concludes a decade‑long legal process that began with the tribunal’s indictment of senior military officials for their roles in the conflict’s most egregious atrocities.

The convicted officer, General Zdravko Tolimir, was held responsible for orchestrating the mass killings at the Srebrenica enclave in July 1995, where more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were executed. The court determined that Tolimir, as chief of staff to the Bosnian Serb Army’s commander, coordinated the deployment of forces that surrounded the UN‑protected town, oversaw the rounding up of civilians, and facilitated their transfer to execution sites. In addition to genocide, the tribunal found him guilty of crimes against humanity and violations of the laws of war, sentencing him to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

The ruling reinforces the international community’s commitment to prosecuting the gravest war crimes and underscores the ICTY’s role in establishing accountability for the Bosnian conflict. Observers note that the conviction may contribute to ongoing reconciliation efforts in the region by affirming that senior leaders can be held personally liable for orchestrating mass atrocities.
author: DW World

title: Ne p floods isolate remote Nepal regions, officials warn of unpreparedness
content:
DW reported on the aftermath of the flash floods that swept through several Nepali districts earlier this week, leaving communities in a state of shock and uncertainty. Survivors described the loss of family members, the destruction of homes, and the sudden disruption of livelihoods as they recounted the harrowing moments when waters surged through villages that had previously seen only seasonal rain. Emergency shelters have been set up in the affected regions, while relief agencies are distributing food, clean water, and medical supplies to those displaced by the disaster.

In a press briefing, a senior government minister acknowledged that the scale of the flooding exceeded the nation’s preparedness, warning that the state was not equipped to handle an event of such magnitude. The minister cited gaps in early warning systems, insufficient infrastructure, and limited resources for rapid response as critical challenges that hampered rescue and relief operations. Authorities have pledged to review disaster management protocols and to seek additional support from international partners to bolster Nepal’s capacity to mitigate future flood risks.
author: DW World

title: Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile surrenders to police, state media reports
content:
Zambia’s national broadcaster reported that opposition presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate surrendered to police authorities early this week. The pair, who had announced plans to contest the results of the recent presidential election, were taken into custody for questioning and are currently being interviewed by law enforcement officials.

According to the broadcaster, the surrender was voluntary and the police have not indicated any charges at this time. The incident follows a period of heightened political activity after the election, during which several opposition figures have sought to challenge the outcome through legal and electoral avenues. The authorities have stated that the interview will focus on the candidates’ intentions and any evidence they may have regarding alleged irregularities.

The situation remains under close observation by both domestic and international observers. While the police have not released further details, the surrender marks a significant development in the post‑election legal process, and the outcome of the interview could influence the trajectory of the opposition’s challenge to the election results.
author: DW World

title: Ratko Mladic, convicted of Srebrenica genocide, dies at 84
content:
Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb commander whose name became synonymous with the atrocities of the Bosnian War, died in detention at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on Tuesday. The 71‑year‑old was found dead in his cell, according to court officials, after a brief hospitalization for an undisclosed illness. His death follows a long legal saga that culminated in his 2017 conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes linked to the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and other violent acts during the conflict.

Mladić’s conviction, delivered by a Dutch court, was upheld by the International Court of Justice in 2018, confirming the charges of genocide and establishing him as the most senior Bosnian Serb leader to be held accountable for the war’s worst crimes. He had been in custody since 2011, when the ICC seized him from Serbia after a failed extradition attempt. His passing marks the end of a case that has been closely followed by international observers, human rights groups and the families of victims, who had long sought closure and justice for the atrocities committed during the war.

The ICC has announced that it will conduct a post‑mortem investigation to determine the exact cause of Mladić’s death. While the court’s officials have not released further details, the organization reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining the integrity of the trial process and ensuring that any findings are made public. The death of Mladić closes a chapter in the pursuit of accountability for the Bosnian War, but the broader implications for international criminal justice and post‑conflict reconciliation remain subjects of ongoing discussion.
author: DW World

title: Bronze Age Gold Collection Stolen from Spain's Villena Museum
content:
A large portion of the Villena Museum’s Bronze Age gold collection was stolen in a swift, four‑minute break‑in that occurred before the museum opened to the public. The thieves entered the premises, accessed the secure display cases, and removed a significant number of artifacts, leaving only a handful of items in place. Security footage captured the group moving quickly and efficiently, suggesting a high level of planning and knowledge of the museum’s layout.

The stolen pieces include several gold objects that are among the finest examples of Bronze Age craftsmanship in the world, valued at millions of euros. According to museum officials, the theft was carried out by a professional group, as evidenced by the careful handling of the artifacts and the absence of damage to the surrounding displays. Police have launched an investigation and are reviewing surveillance footage from nearby businesses to identify the perpetrators.

Authorities have urged the public to come forward with any information that could aid the recovery of the missing artifacts. The museum has pledged to cooperate fully with law enforcement and to enhance security measures to prevent future incidents. The loss of these cultural treasures is a significant blow to heritage preservation and underscores the ongoing threat to historic collections worldwide.
author: DW World

title: Hundreds missing after Himalayan flood hits Nepal and China, aid teams mobilize
content:
A sudden surge of floodwater struck towns and villages in the border regions of Nepal and China on Wednesday, leaving officials to report that hundreds of residents remain missing. The flash flooding, triggered by unusually heavy monsoon rains that caused several rivers to overflow, inundated low‑lying settlements and swept away homes, vehicles and infrastructure. Local authorities in both countries have launched search operations, but the scale of the disaster and the rugged terrain have hampered immediate rescue efforts, raising concerns about the fate of those still unaccounted for.

Humanitarian agencies and government rescue teams have mobilized to reach communities isolated by washed‑out roads and landslides, deploying helicopters, boats and ground crews to deliver food, medical supplies and temporary shelter. Coordination between Nepalese and Chinese disaster‑response units aims to prioritize the most vulnerable areas while establishing safe corridors for evacuation. As the floodwaters recede, officials continue to assess damage, update missing‑person counts and plan longer‑term recovery measures for the affected populations.
author: UN News

title: UN official urges international aid for Syria's post-war reconstruction
content:
Damascus is embarking on a large‑scale reconstruction effort after more than ten years of conflict, a process that has been complicated by recent political shifts such as the dissolution of the Kurdish‑led Syrian Democratic Forces and the United States’ decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. In a briefing to the United Nations Security Council on Thursday, a senior UN official highlighted that while the Syrian government is making progress in rebuilding infrastructure and restoring basic services, significant gaps remain in areas such as de‑mining, housing, health care and the reintegration of displaced populations.

The UN representative urged member states to sustain and expand international assistance, emphasizing that coordinated financial aid, technical expertise and humanitarian support are essential to address the lingering challenges and to ensure a stable, inclusive recovery. The official’s remarks underscored the Council’s role in mobilizing resources and monitoring implementation, calling for a continued global commitment to Syria’s post‑war reconstruction.
author: UN News

title: UN warns civilians at risk in south Lebanon amid Israeli-Hezbollah strikes
content:
South Lebanon remains in a state of heightened danger as the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) reports ongoing damage to infrastructure and civilian services amid continued clashes between Israeli forces and Hezbollah. According to the mission’s latest assessment, roads have been severely damaged, impeding movement and access to essential services for local residents.

The UN report highlights that the frequent strikes and military activity have disrupted utilities, healthcare, and supply chains, leaving civilians exposed to additional risks. UNIFIL officials emphasized that the deteriorating conditions are exacerbating the humanitarian situation, with many families facing shortages of clean water, electricity, and medical care.

UNIFIL continues to monitor the situation closely, urging all parties to minimize civilian harm and restore stability in the region. The mission’s findings underscore the urgent need for a durable ceasefire to protect the safety and well‑being of the civilian population in south Lebanon.
author: UN News

title: Israeli strike kills woman in Nabatieh, southern Lebanon
content:
Israeli airstrikes on the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh resulted in the death of a Lebanese woman and injured several other civilians, local authorities reported. The attacks, which targeted residential areas in the city, caused significant damage to private homes and infrastructure, prompting emergency services to respond to the scene and transport the wounded to nearby hospitals.

The incident occurs amid heightened tensions along the Israel‑Lebanon border, where periodic exchanges of fire have escalated in recent weeks. Lebanese officials have condemned the strikes as violations of international law, while Israeli statements have linked the operations to ongoing security concerns. The latest casualties add to the growing humanitarian impact of the cross‑border hostilities, underscoring the fragile stability in the region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Zambia judiciary closes, final day to challenge Hichilema's election win
content:
Zambia’s judiciary shut its doors on Monday, marking the final day for any court challenge to President‑elect Hakainde Hichilema’s election victory. The closure came after the Supreme Court’s deadline for filing petitions expired, leaving the electoral outcome unaltered. The decision effectively ended the legal avenue for opposition parties to contest the results.

The challenge, lodged by the United Party for National Development (UPND) and its allies, alleged irregularities in the voting process and questioned the validity of certain ballots. However, the court rejected the petitions on procedural grounds, citing the failure to meet the statutory filing window. With the judiciary closed, the ruling party’s claim of a legitimate win stands unchallenged.

The finality of the court’s decision confirms Hichilema’s status as Zambia’s president, concluding the post‑election legal dispute and allowing the new administration to proceed with its agenda.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump Executive Order Bans Foreign Equipment in U.S. Energy Grid
content:
Washington — The White House issued an executive order on Monday declaring a national emergency in response to what officials described as an “unusual and extraordinary foreign threat” to the United States electric grid. The order, signed by President Joe Biden, invokes emergency powers under the National Emergencies Act and directs the Department of Energy, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to coordinate a rapid assessment of vulnerabilities, accelerate the deployment of protective technologies, and prioritize funding for grid hardening projects.

The declaration follows a series of high‑profile cyber intrusions attributed to state‑linked actors, including attempts to infiltrate utility control systems and the deployment of sophisticated malware targeting supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) networks. The administration cited intelligence reports indicating that adversaries have developed capabilities to disrupt power transmission on a large scale, prompting concerns about potential blackouts and cascading impacts on critical services. Under the order, agencies will issue mandatory cybersecurity standards for bulk power operators, expand information‑sharing with private sector partners, and seek congressional approval for additional emergency funding to bolster resilience. The move signals a heightened federal focus on safeguarding the nation’s energy infrastructure amid escalating geopolitical tensions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Children treated for smoke-related breathing problems at Indonesian clinic amid wildfires
content:
Al Jazeera correspondent Jessica Washington reported from a temporary clinic in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, where medical staff are treating a growing number of children experiencing respiratory distress as thick haze from regional wildfires lingers over the province. The clinic, set up by the local health department in collaboration with the Indonesian Ministry of Health, has admitted more than 120 pediatric patients since the haze intensified three days ago, with doctors noting a sharp rise in cases of asthma exacerbations, bronchitis and other breathing difficulties. Officials attribute the haze to uncontrolled slash‑and‑burn practices in nearby peatlands, which have ignited extensive forest fires that are producing fine particulate matter (PM2.5) well above World Health Organization safety thresholds.

Health authorities are distributing masks, conducting air‑quality monitoring and advising families to keep children indoors, while the Ministry of Environment and Forestry works to contain the fires and prevent further spread. The clinic’s staff, supported by volunteers from the Red Cross, are providing oxygen therapy and inhaled bronchodilators, and are coordinating with regional hospitals for any severe cases that require advanced care. As the haze persists, officials warn that the health impact could extend beyond the current surge, urging continued vigilance and rapid response to the underlying fire activity.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Beluga whales and dolphins moved from Canada’s Marineland to Spanish aquarium
content:
Two beluga whales and four dolphins that had been housed at Canada’s Marineland in Ontario were transferred to a marine aquarium in Spain, according to a statement released by the facility’s management. The animals were moved as part of a planned program to relocate marine mammals to more suitable long‑term care environments. The Spanish aquarium, located in the coastal city of Valencia, has the capacity to provide the specialized enclosures and veterinary support required for these large cetaceans.

The transfer was carried out under strict veterinary supervision, with the animals transported in climate‑controlled containers and monitored throughout the journey. Marineland officials noted that the decision was driven by a combination of factors, including the aging infrastructure of the Canadian facility and the aquarium’s commitment to conservation and rehabilitation. The Spanish institution will house the belugas and dolphins in state‑of‑the‑art tanks designed to mimic their natural habitats, and will collaborate with marine biologists to ensure their health and well‑being.

The relocation is expected to enhance the welfare of the animals and provide them with a more appropriate environment for their species. Both Marineland and the Spanish aquarium have pledged to maintain open communication regarding the animals’ progress and to share research findings that could benefit broader marine conservation efforts.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Indonesia Wildfires Threaten Health in West Kalimantan
content:
Health officials in West Kalimantan have reported a sharp rise in respiratory and related ailments as widespread fires continue to generate dense smoke across the province. Air quality monitoring stations recorded particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations exceeding safe limits for several consecutive days, prompting the regional health agency to issue advisories urging residents to limit outdoor activities and to use protective masks. Hospitals in the capital, Pontianak, and surrounding districts have seen an influx of patients presenting with coughing, shortness of breath, and eye irritation, with doctors noting that the most severe cases involve pregnant women and children, who are particularly susceptible to the pollutants.

Local authorities have mobilized fire‑fighting teams and coordinated with neighboring provinces to contain the blazes, while the Ministry of Environment and Forestry has pledged additional resources for aerial water drops and forest management. Public health officials are distributing informational leaflets and establishing temporary clinics in affected communities to monitor vulnerable groups and provide early treatment. As the fire season progresses, officials stress that continued monitoring and community cooperation will be essential to mitigate health risks and prevent further deterioration of air quality in West Kalimantan.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Supreme Court upholds mail‑in ballot restrictions, USPS says they are now in effect
content:
The U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling that upheld a set of changes to election procedures that had been championed by former President Donald Trump. In a 5‑to‑4 decision, the Court found that the modifications—ranging from stricter voter ID requirements to alterations in mail‑ballot verification—were consistent with the Constitution and did not violate federal voting‑rights statutes. The majority opinion cited state sovereignty over election administration and argued that the changes did not impose an undue burden on voters.

Despite the Court’s endorsement, several new legal challenges have been filed in federal courts across the country. Plaintiffs, including civil‑rights groups and state officials, argue that the reforms disproportionately affect minority and low‑income voters and that the evidence presented to the Supreme Court was incomplete. The lawsuits seek injunctions to block the implementation of the contested provisions while the cases are reviewed, potentially setting the stage for further appellate action.

The outcome of these fresh suits could reshape the enforcement of the Supreme Court’s decision and influence how the changes are applied in upcoming elections. Observers note that the legal battles underscore ongoing national debates over election integrity, voter access, and the balance between state authority and federal oversight.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order today that officially renames Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” The directive, issued under the authority of the President’s power to rename federal geographic features, changes the name of the 7th‑largest lake in the United States, which borders New York State and Ontario, Canada. The order directs the U.S. Geological Survey to update all federal maps and documents to reflect the new name and to coordinate with state and local agencies for the transition.

Lake Ontario has long been a key part of the Great Lakes system, supporting commerce, recreation, and cross‑border water agreements. The renaming follows a brief statement from the White House that the change is intended to “highlight the lake’s significance to the American people.” No legislative action was required, and the order does not alter any legal or environmental regulations tied to the lake. The U.S. Department of the Interior will oversee the implementation and will issue further guidance on how the new name will be adopted in federal and state contexts.

The executive order has sparked discussion among stakeholders, including Canadian officials who oversee the shared waterway, and local residents who have identified with the historic name. While the directive is legally binding for federal use, its adoption at the state and local levels will depend on subsequent coordination. The White House has not announced any immediate plans to address potential opposition or to engage in a broader public consultation process.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Jerusalem court acquits man who attacked nun, citing psychotic episode
content:
A Jerusalem district court ruled that the Jewish man who attacked a Catholic nun in the city’s Old Quarter was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time of the assault. The incident, which occurred last month when the nun was walking to a nearby convent, sparked widespread condemnation from religious leaders and community groups, who described the attack as an act of violence against a figure of peace. The court’s assessment was based on psychiatric evaluations presented during the hearing, which indicated that the defendant’s mental state impaired his ability to discern right from wrong.

The judge ordered the attacker to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment and imposed a custodial sentence that reflects both the severity of the crime and the mitigating factor of his mental illness. Israeli police and the Ministry of Justice emphasized that the ruling underscores the legal system’s responsibility to address violent offenses while ensuring appropriate care for individuals with severe mental health conditions. The decision aims to balance public safety concerns with the need for treatment, concluding a case that had drawn significant public attention and heightened interfaith sensitivities.
author: BBC World

title: Two dead, 19-year-old arrested after domestic violence incident at school near Berlin
content:
Police arrested a 19‑year‑old male suspect following a fatal incident that took place near Berlin, the German capital. The arrest came after authorities received reports of a shooting that resulted in the deaths of two individuals in the outskirts of the city.

Investigators say the suspect was apprehended at a nearby location shortly after the incident. While details of the motive and the circumstances surrounding the killings remain under investigation, police confirmed that the suspect is being held on charges related to the murders. The case is being handled by the Berlin police department in cooperation with federal prosecutors.

The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are continuing to gather evidence. No further information has been released at this time.
author: BBC World

title: Peace Board envoy warns ceasefire collapse could be point of no return
content:
Nickolay Mladenov, the United Nations special envoy for Syria, warned on Tuesday that the disintegration of the ceasefire brokered in October would represent “a point of no return” for the war‑torn region. The ceasefire, which was intended to halt hostilities between the Syrian government and opposition forces and to create space for humanitarian aid, has been under strain amid renewed fighting in several provinces and accusations of violations by both sides.

Mladenov emphasized that a collapse of the truce could trigger a rapid escalation of violence, undermine diplomatic initiatives, and deepen the humanitarian crisis that has already displaced millions. He called on all parties to respect the agreement and urged the international community to reinforce monitoring mechanisms to prevent further breakdowns. The envoy’s statement comes as regional actors and UN partners intensify efforts to sustain the fragile peace and avert a broader destabilization of the Middle East.
author: BBC World

title: Jury deliberates in trial of Lindsay Clancy accused of killing her children
content:
Prosecutors at the trial contended that the defendant, identified as Clancy, acted with deliberation in the killing of her children, presenting evidence they say demonstrates a calculated decision to commit the murders. The prosecution’s case emphasized pre‑meditated actions and motive, seeking to establish that the homicides were the result of conscious intent rather than a momentary lapse.

In contrast, Clancy’s defense team argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the offenses, asserting that the severe mental illness impaired her judgment and capacity to control her behavior. The defense highlighted medical testimony regarding the condition’s impact on perception and decision‑making, aiming to mitigate responsibility. The court will consider both arguments as it moves toward a verdict.
author: BBC World

title: Bosnian Serb war criminal Radovan Mladić dies at 84
content:
A court sentenced the former Bosnian Serb official to life imprisonment in 2017 after finding him guilty of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1992‑1995 conflicts that accompanied the breakup of Yugoslavia. The verdict concluded a lengthy trial that examined evidence of systematic killings, forced displacement and other atrocities perpetrated against civilian populations in the region.

The life sentence reflects the gravity of the offenses, which were part of a broader pattern of ethnic violence that marked the wars in the former Yugoslav republics. International tribunals continue to pursue accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, underscoring the ongoing commitment to justice for victims of the Balkan conflicts.
author: BBC World

title: Creamfields 2026 Marks 20th Anniversary at Daresbury
content:
The four‑day dance‑music festival in Daresbury, Cheshire, marks its 20th anniversary this year. The event, held annually at the historic Daresbury Hall and surrounding grounds, has become a staple of the UK club scene, drawing thousands of fans from across the country.

Organisers have highlighted a lineup that spans the genre’s evolution, featuring both veteran DJs and emerging talent. The festival’s schedule includes multiple stages and themed nights, with the main stage hosting headline acts and the smaller venues showcasing niche sub‑genres. Attendance figures for the 2024 edition are expected to match or exceed previous years, reflecting the event’s sustained popularity.

As the festival concludes, organisers will review its impact on the local community and the broader dance‑music landscape. The 20th‑year celebration underscores the event’s longevity and its role in sustaining the cultural vitality of Cheshire’s music scene.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Biopic, coffee brand and dog treats among Dolly Parton's upcoming business projects
content:
Dolly, the celebrated performer whose career spanned more than three decades, passed away last week at the age of 58. In a brief statement released by her manager, it was confirmed that Dolly worked continuously up until the day of her death, continuing rehearsals and recording sessions for her final projects. The manager noted that Dolly’s dedication to her craft remained unwavering, even as she faced health challenges in the months prior.

Following Dolly’s passing, her management team announced that several projects slated for release in the coming months will be made available posthumously. These include a new studio album, a collection of unreleased live recordings, and a documentary chronicling her career. The releases are scheduled to honor Dolly’s legacy and provide fans with a final glimpse into her artistry.

The announcement has prompted widespread reflection on Dolly’s influence in the music industry, with colleagues and fans alike expressing gratitude for her contributions. While the loss is deeply felt, the forthcoming releases are intended to preserve her memory and celebrate the body of work she left behind.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Top Gear to return after Flintoff crash, BBC confirms
content:
The popular daytime program *The Daily Exchange* was put on hold after co‑host Andrew Flintoff sustained serious injuries in a vehicle accident that occurred during a 2022 filming session. The crash, which took place on a rural road near the studio’s location, left Flintoff with fractures to his left arm and a concussion, according to the production team.

Following the incident, the network announced that the show would be “rested” while Flintoff received medical treatment and recovered. Production halted all on‑location shoots and the remaining episodes were postponed, with the studio shifting to a temporary digital format to keep the audience engaged. The decision was made in consultation with Flintoff’s management and the network’s health and safety department.

The network has not yet confirmed a return date for *The Daily Exchange*. In the interim, it has pledged to keep viewers informed of Flintoff’s progress and any updates regarding the program’s resumption.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Carse in the wickets for Durham, Essex v Surrey, and more: county cricket day one – live
content:
The County Championship opened with the England v Pakistan second Test at Scarborough, where the early action was dominated by a quick wicket. Adam Lyth was dismissed on the sixth ball of the innings, his dismissal coming on a mottled outfield that had been a talking point for the day. The wicket gave Yorkshire a 5‑1 advantage early in the match, setting a brisk tone for the rest of the day.

Gloucestershire’s Joe Phillips was the first bowler to take a wicket, claiming his sixth ball of the game in a spell that highlighted the pitch’s uneven nature. In the lead‑up to the match, the OBO team encouraged fans to get in touch with Tanya via email or BTLShackles for further information and updates. These channels have been used to relay real‑time commentary and player insights throughout the day's play.

As the match progressed, the early momentum gained by England’s bowlers continued to pressure the Pakistani batting lineup. With Yorkshire holding a 5‑1 lead, the teams are expected to trade wickets in the coming sessions, making the remainder of the day a contest for both sides to establish dominance in the second Test.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Itauma to Challenge Hrgovic for IBF Heavyweight Title
content:
Moses Itauma, 21, will face Croatia’s Filip Hrgovic for the IBF world heavyweight title at the O2 Arena in London on Saturday night, with the bout positioned as a potential milestone that could make the British prospect the second‑youngest champion in history after Mike Tyson. The Guardian has sought the opinions of boxing analysts Barry Jones and Andy Lee to separate the hype from the fighter’s actual abilities.

Jones and Lee highlighted Itauma’s unbeaten record and his rapid ascent to the top of the heavyweight rankings, noting that his power and speed have already made him a threat in the division. They also pointed out that Hrgovic, in just his 15th professional fight, presents the first serious test of Itauma’s skill against an experienced world‑champion‑level opponent. The experts suggested that while Itauma’s confidence is high, the match will expose any gaps in his technique and conditioning that could be exploited by a seasoned contender.

The fight is expected to be a defining moment for the young British boxer, who has vowed to become a dominant force in the unpredictable heavyweight scene. Whether he can translate his early success into a world‑championship victory against Hrgovic remains to be seen, but the encounter is already shaping up to be a key chapter in the sport’s current narrative.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Linda Noskova Wins Wimbledon, Faces New Challenges
content:
Linda Noskova, the Czech‑born tennis player who captured the Wimbledon women’s singles title last month, has long balanced her on‑court ambitions with a range of off‑court interests. Growing up in Czechia, she began competing across the country and Europe before turning professional as a teenager, and has since travelled worldwide for tournaments. Her victory at the 2023 Wimbledon Championships marked the culmination of a career that has been defined by disciplined training and early international exposure.

The triumph, while a personal dream realised, has also highlighted the challenges of life after a major title. Noskova has acknowledged that the world did not pause once the final point was played; she now faces the task of redefining her role within the sport and managing the expectations that accompany her new status. As she reflects on her journey—from Czech courts to the global stage—she is looking to integrate her tennis career with her broader passions, seeking a sustainable path that balances competition with personal growth.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Pogba and Sancho's struggles warn Carrick's rebuild
content:
Bruno Fernandes remains the sole surviving attacker from Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s 2021 summer overhaul of Manchester United.  The season began with high expectations after a 5‑1 victory over Leeds, a sign that the club was on the cusp of a genuine title challenge.  Solskjaer’s plans included the marquee signing of Cristiano Ronaldo, the acquisition of young English talent Jadon Sancho, and the continued partnership of Fernandes with Paul Pogba as the team’s creative fulcrum.

Despite the optimism, the signings did not deliver the desired results.  Ronaldo’s arrival was seen as a symbolic step toward bridging the gap to rivals, but the team struggled to maintain momentum in the months that followed.  Fernandes, however, remained a consistent presence on the pitch, contributing goals and assists while the rest of the attacking line saw a rapid turnover of players.

Today, Fernandes’ continued role at Old Trafford highlights the lasting impact of Solskjaer’s 2021 strategy.  His presence serves as a tangible link to that pivotal summer, underscoring how the club’s ambitions and the players who embodied them have evolved over the past five years.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Liam Delap signs record £45m deal with Nottingham Forest
content:
Nottingham Forest have secured a club‑record signing with the acquisition of Chelsea striker Liam Delap for £45 million. The 23‑year‑old, who scored twice after joining the Blues last season, had been sidelined by Xabi Alonso’s plans and is now set to begin a five‑year contract with Forest’s new manager Oliver Glasner. Delap’s arrival marks the third club move in three seasons for the forward, who expressed enthusiasm about the opportunity to develop under Glasner’s guidance and contribute goals to the team.

Delap’s transfer comes as Forest look to bolster their attacking options following a challenging campaign. The club’s record fee underscores the confidence placed in the young striker’s potential, with Glasner citing Delap as a priority during the transfer window. The player highlighted the club’s rich history and the manager’s approach, stating that he believes Glasner can help him reach the next level of his career.

With the deal completed, Forest now have a proven goal‑scorer to support their push for promotion. Delap’s five‑year commitment signals a long‑term plan to strengthen the squad, while the club’s willingness to invest a record sum reflects their ambition to return to the Premier League. The signing is expected to add firepower to Forest’s attack as they prepare for the upcoming season.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England vs Pakistan Test delayed, toss set for 12pm BST
content:
County cricket at Lord’s is underway, with the liveblog updating spectators over‑by‑over from 11:00 BST. The match, featuring the county teams, is being covered in real time, allowing fans to follow the action as it unfolds across the grounds. Readers can join the discussion by signing up for “The Spin” newsletter or by emailing Taha for further updates.

The toss is scheduled for 12:00 BST, with play to commence at 12:20. This timing aligns with the traditional schedule for County fixtures at Lord’s, giving teams a brief interval to decide batting or bowling first. The liveblog will capture the outcome of the toss and the initial overs, providing detailed commentary and statistics for viewers.

As the game progresses, the liveblog will continue to deliver concise, factual updates on scores, wickets, and key moments. Fans following the coverage can stay informed about the match’s developments and receive timely notifications through the newsletter or direct email contact.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Esther Gonzalez signs with Saudi club amid fan backlash
content:
Spanish forward Esther González has drawn criticism after agreeing to join Al Qadsiah of the Saudi Women’s Premier League. The 26‑year‑old, who has represented Spain at youth levels and played professionally in Spain’s Primera Femenina, signed a one‑year contract with the Riyadh‑based club in early August. The move comes as the Saudi league, which launched in 2022, continues to attract foreign talent amid a broader push to develop women’s football in the Kingdom.

González’s decision has sparked backlash among Spanish supporters and football commentators, who cite concerns over the league’s cultural restrictions and the perceived lack of competitive standards compared to Europe. Critics argue that the move could hinder her development and reduce her visibility on the international stage. Supporters of the transfer, however, point to the financial incentives and the opportunity to pioneer a growing sport in a new market.

The transfer underscores the growing trend of European players exploring opportunities in emerging football markets. While González’s future impact in Saudi Arabia remains to be seen, her signing highlights the expanding global reach of women’s football and the complex choices players face between competitive ambition and commercial opportunity.
author: BBC Sport

title: Delap joins Forest for £50m bidding to rebuild career
content:
BBC Sport’s recent feature on former Burnley midfielder Liam Delap focuses on the factors that stalled his progress at Chelsea and outlines a path for his resurgence in a new environment. Delap joined the Premier League club in 2015 with high expectations, but a combination of limited first‑team opportunities, recurring injuries and a tactical mismatch with the squad’s midfield setup curtailed his impact. The piece notes that, despite occasional flashes of his creative flair, he struggled to cement a regular spot amid stiff competition from established midfielders and a system that favored a more defensive, possession‑oriented approach.

The article suggests that a move to a club offering more consistent playing time and a role that better suits his skill set could reignite Delap’s career. By returning to a league where his passing range and vision are prized, and by focusing on regaining full fitness and confidence, Delap could reestablish himself as a key contributor. BBC Sport concludes that, with the right environment and support, the former England international has the potential to return to the form that first attracted Chelsea’s interest.
author: BBC Sport

title: How to follow Thursday's Champions League draw - and who is in each pot?
content:
BBC Sport’s Ask Me Anything team has answered a flurry of questions about the upcoming 2026‑27 UEFA Champions League, revealing that the league‑phase draw will take place on **30 August 2026** at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland. The draw will be streamed live, with the 32 clubs that have progressed from the group stage being allocated to the knockout rounds in a standard bracket format.

The pots for the draw will be seeded by the UEFA club coefficients, with the champions of the top five associations occupying Pot 1 (England, Spain, Italy, Germany and France). Pot 2 will contain the champions of the next five associations (Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands, Turkey and Austria). Pot 3 will feature the champions of the following five (Switzerland, Poland, the Czech Republic, Denmark and Sweden), while Pot 4 will hold the champions of the remaining five (Romania, Greece, Croatia, Slovenia and Scotland). Each pot will be drawn in turn, ensuring a balanced mix of clubs from across Europe in the knockout phase.

With the draw date now confirmed, clubs and fans can begin to plan for the next stage of Europe’s premier club competition, knowing exactly when and how the match‑ups will be determined.
author: BBC Sport

title: Liverpool Near £120m Deal for PSG's Bradley Barcola
content:
Liverpool are reportedly nearing a deal to sign Paris Saint‑Germain midfielder Bradley Barcola, a move that could deepen uncertainty over the future of striker Cody Gakpo.  The French club has agreed on a transfer fee with Liverpool, with the two sides finalising the terms of Barcola’s move, according to club officials.  The midfielder, who has been a key creative force for PSG, would bring a new dimension to Anfield’s midfield and could prompt a reshuffle of the squad’s attacking options.

Gakpo’s status at Liverpool has been unclear since the summer, with the Dutch forward’s contract set to expire at the end of the season.  The club’s interest in Barcola has raised speculation that Gakpo may be on the transfer list or could be moved to accommodate the new signing.  Liverpool’s management has yet to confirm whether Gakpo’s future will involve a new contract, a loan, or a permanent transfer to another club.  The club’s decision on Barcola’s arrival is likely to influence the final resolution of Gakpo’s situation.
author: BBC Sport

title: Derbyshire Police Investigate Alleged Assault on Brydon Carse
content:
Derbyshire Police are investigating an incident in which Brydon Carse was handcuffed, following allegations that he was assaulted during the event. title: Texas House Candidate Jorge Borrego Apologizes for Crude Online Posts
content:
Jorge Borrego, a candidate for the Texas State House, issued a public apology on Wednesday for a series of social‑media posts that contained “crude and immature jokes.” The apology followed a brief period earlier in the week when Borrego had dismissed the content as a joke, but the backlash prompted him to address the issue directly.

In his statement, Borrego clarified that the posts do not reflect his current beliefs or values. He explained that the remarks were influenced by his childhood environment, a factor he said shaped his early humor but is no longer representative of his perspective. The candidate emphasized that his campaign is focused on policy and community service, and that the past posts are a matter of the past.

Borrego’s apology comes as he continues to run for the Texas House, where he faces scrutiny over his social‑media conduct. The candidate’s quick response and acknowledgement of the issue are intended to mitigate the impact on his campaign, though the long‑term effect on voter perception remains to be seen.

title: Josh Turek Rejects Harris Campaigning for Him
content:
Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek dismissed the possibility of former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning for him at a Wednesday event in Cedar Rapids. The state representative, who has served in the Iowa House and won two Paralympic basketball gold medals, was asked by a reporter about the prospect of working with Harris during his campaign. Turek replied that he would not seek or accept a campaign appearance from the former vice president.

Turek’s comments came amid a broader push for the Senate seat, as the Democratic field seeks to build momentum in a state that has recently leaned Republican in statewide contests. The candidate’s background as a Paralympic athlete and legislator has been a focal point of his campaign messaging, emphasizing public service and resilience. He reiterated that his campaign strategy will rely on local grassroots efforts and direct voter engagement rather than high‑profile endorsements.

The statement underscores Turek’s intent to maintain an independent campaign approach. He remains focused on addressing Iowa voters’ concerns on issues such as healthcare, education, and economic development, while continuing to build support within the Democratic electorate.
